why.D: This takes x = −5, the axis with its sign reversed, which lowers the price.

context: For which values of k does x² + kx + 9 = 0 have no real solutions?

why.A: This is where the discriminant is positive, which gives two real solutions.
why.B: Correct — there are no real solutions when the discriminant k² − 36 is negative, which is when k² < 36.
why.C: This uses k² < 9, taking the constant term without the factor of 4 in 4ac.
why.D: This solves k < 6 and forgets that k² < 36 also needs k > −6. At k = −10 there are two real solutions.

context: In right triangle PQR, the right angle is at R, PR = 7, QR = 24 and PQ = 25. What is cos P?

why.A: This is sin P: the side opposite P over the hypotenuse.
why.B: This is the adjacent leg over the opposite leg, which is the tangent of angle Q. Cosine uses the hypotenuse.
why.C: Correct — cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse. The leg next to P is PR = 7, and the hypotenuse is PQ = 25.
why.D: This divides the hypotenuse by the adjacent leg, the reciprocal of cos P.

context: An angle in standard position measures 210°. In which quadrant does its terminal side lie?

why.A: Quadrant II runs from 90° to 180°; 210° is already past 180°.
why.B: Quadrant IV runs from 270° to 360°; 210° has not reached 270°.
why.C: This subtracts 180° and places the 30° that is left, which is the reference angle, not the angle itself.
why.D: Correct — 210° is between 180° and 270°, which is Quadrant III.

context: In a right triangle, A and B are the two acute angles, and sin A = 0.6. What is cos B?

why.A: Correct — the side opposite A is the side adjacent to B, and both ratios use the same hypotenuse, so cos B = sin A.
why.B: This is cos A, which is √(1 − 0.36). The question asks about angle B.
why.C: This subtracts 0.6 from 1. Sines and cosines of complementary angles are equal, not complements of 1.
why.D: This is tan A, 0.6 ÷ 0.8.

context: A wheelchair ramp is 24 feet long, measured along its sloped surface, and it rises 2 feet. Which expression gives the angle θ the ramp makes with the ground?

why.A: This treats 24 feet as the horizontal distance. The ramp is measured along its slope, which is the hypotenuse.
why.B: Correct — the rise is opposite θ and the ramp’s 24-foot surface is the hypotenuse, so sin θ = 2/24 = 1/12.
why.C: Cosine uses the side adjacent to θ, the ground distance, not the 2-foot rise.
why.D: This inverts the ratio. A sine can never be greater than 1.

context: What is the range of the function y = 3 sin x + 1?

why.A: This applies the amplitude of 3 but not the upward shift of 1.
why.B: This shifts the graph down 1 instead of up.
why.C: Correct — sin x runs from −1 to 1, so 3 sin x runs from −3 to 3, and adding 1 gives −2 to 4.
why.D: This starts the range at the midline, 1. The graph goes 3 below the midline as well as 3 above it.

context: For cos θ ≠ 1, which expression is equal to sin²θ / (1 − cos θ)?

why.A: This writes sin²θ as (1 − cos θ)². The identity gives 1 − cos²θ, which factors differently.
why.B: This replaces sin²θ with 1 − cos θ, dropping the square on the cosine.
why.C: This factors 1 − cos²θ as (cos θ − 1)(cos θ + 1) and cancels as if cos θ − 1 were 1 − cos θ, losing a sign.
why.D: Correct — sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ = (1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ), and the factor 1 − cos θ cancels.

context: A 25-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall and reaches 24 feet up the wall. What is the tangent of the angle the ladder makes with the ground?

why.A: Correct — the foot of the ladder is √(25² − 24²) = 7 feet from the wall, so the tangent is 24/7.
why.B: This divides the ground distance by the height, which is the tangent of the angle at the top of the ladder.
why.C: This is the sine of the angle: height over the ladder’s length.
why.D: This is the cosine of the angle: ground distance over the ladder’s length.

context: The graph of y = cos x is shifted π/2 units to the right. Which equation describes the new graph?

why.A: This is cos(x + π/2), a shift to the left.
why.B: Correct — the new graph is y = cos(x − π/2), and cos(x − π/2) = sin x: the sine curve is the cosine curve a quarter-period later.
why.C: This is a shift of π, a half-period, not π/2.
why.D: This shifts the graph down by π/2. A horizontal shift changes the input, not the output.

context: In triangle ABC, angle A measures 40°, angle B measures 75°, and side a, opposite angle A, has length 10. Which expression gives the length of side c?

why.A: This uses angle B, which gives side b. Side c needs the angle opposite it, C.
why.B: This inverts the ratio. Multiplying by sin C / sin A scales a up to c, not the reverse.
why.C: Correct — angle C = 180° − 40° − 75° = 65°, and the law of sines gives c/sin 65° = 10/sin 40°.
why.D: This pairs side a with angle B, but a is opposite angle A.

context: What are all solutions of 2 sin x − 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ x < 360°?

why.A: This stops at the first solution. Sine is also positive in Quadrant II.
why.B: This reflects 30° as a cosine solution would be reflected. In Quadrant IV sine is negative.
why.C: These solve cos x = 1/2, not sin x = 1/2.
why.D: Correct — sin x = 1/2, and sine is positive in Quadrants I and II, so x = 30° or 180° − 30° = 150°.

context: Two people stand on level ground in a straight line with the base of a tower, 100 meters apart. From the nearer person the angle of elevation to the top is 45°, and from the farther person it is 30°. How tall is the tower, in meters?

why.A: Correct — with height h, the nearer person is h meters away (45°), so tan 30° = h/(h + 100). Then h√3 = h + 100, and h = 100/(√3 − 1) = 50(√3 + 1).
why.B: This assumes the nearer person is 100 meters from the tower. The 100 meters is the gap between the two people.
why.C: This sets up h = 100/(√3 − 1) but rationalizes with the wrong sign.
why.D: This uses only the 30° angle and treats the 100-meter gap as the whole distance to the tower.

context: For an acute angle θ, tan θ = 2. What is the value of sin θ · cos θ?

why.A: This is sin θ alone, before multiplying by cos θ = 1/√5.
why.B: Correct — take legs 2 and 1, so the hypotenuse is √5. Then sin θ cos θ = (2/√5)(1/√5) = 2/5.
why.C: This is sin²θ, squaring the sine instead of multiplying it by the cosine.
why.D: This takes the hypotenuse as 1 + 2 = 3 instead of √(1² + 2²).

context: A linear function f has f(1) = 3, f(2) = 5, f(3) = 7 and f(4) = 9. Which expression defines f(x)?

why.A: This matches f(1) = 3 but rises by only 1 per step.
why.B: This matches f(1) = 3 but rises by 3 per step.
why.C: Correct — the values rise by 2 for each step in x, and 2(1) + 1 = 3 matches the first value.
why.D: This takes the first value, 3, as the constant term. That would make f(0) = 3, but f(0) is 1.

context: The graph of y = f(x) is shifted 5 units down. Which equation describes the new graph?

why.A: This shifts the graph 5 units to the right.
why.B: This shifts the graph 5 units to the left.
why.C: This shifts the graph 5 units up.
why.D: Correct — subtracting 5 from every output moves each point 5 units down.

context: What is the minimum value of f(x) = |x − 3| + 2?

why.A: Correct — |x − 3| is never less than 0 and equals 0 at x = 3, so the least value of f is 0 + 2 = 2.
why.B: This is where the minimum occurs, x = 3, not the minimum value of f.
why.C: This is f(0) = 3 + 2, the y-intercept, which is not the lowest point of the V.
why.D: This is the minimum of |x − 3| before the 2 is added.

context: If f(x) = x² + 1 and g(x) = 3x − 2, which expression is equal to g(f(x))?

why.A: This is f(g(x)) = (3x − 2)² + 1, the composition in the other order.
why.B: Correct — g(f(x)) = 3(x² + 1) − 2 = 3x² + 3 − 2 = 3x² + 1.
why.C: This multiplies f(x) by g(x) instead of putting f(x) into g.
why.D: This multiplies only x² by 3, getting 3x² + 1 − 2. The 3 multiplies all of x² + 1.

context: The graph of f(x) = 3x + 2 is reflected across the y-axis. Which function describes the reflected graph?

why.A: This is −f(x), the reflection across the x-axis.
why.B: This reflects across both axes, which is −f(−x).
why.C: Correct — reflecting across the y-axis replaces x with −x: f(−x) = 3(−x) + 2.
why.D: This is the inverse function, the reflection across the line y = x.

context: What is the range of f(x) = x² − 4x?

why.A: This is the range of x² alone. Subtracting 4x lowers the vertex below the x-axis.
why.B: This uses the x-coordinate of the vertex as the lowest output.
why.C: An upward-opening parabola has a lowest point, so its outputs are bounded below.
why.D: Correct — x² − 4x = (x − 2)² − 4, so the lowest output is −4, at x = 2, and the parabola opens upward.

context: The function f is defined by f(x) = x² for x < 1 and f(x) = 3 − x for x ≥ 1. What is f(−2) + f(4)?

why.B: This uses 3 − x for both inputs: 5 + (−1).
why.C: This uses x² for both inputs: 4 + 16.
why.D: This swaps the rules, using 3 − x for −2 and x² for 4: 5 + 16.

context: For which values of x is f(x) = (x − 3)/(x² − 9) undefined?

why.A: This cancels x − 3 first. The simplified form 1/(x + 3) agrees with f everywhere except x = 3, where f itself is still undefined.
why.B: Correct — the denominator x² − 9 is zero at both x = 3 and x = −3, and division by zero is undefined at each.
why.C: This sets the numerator’s factor to zero. A zero numerator is allowed; only the denominator matters.
why.D: This solves x² − 9 = 0 as x = ±9, forgetting to take the square root of 9.

context: Let f(x) = 2x − 3, and let g be the inverse function of f. What is the value of g(f(g(5)))?

why.A: This cancels too much. f(g(5)) is 5, but the outer g still has to be applied to it.
why.B: This is f(5) = 2(5) − 3, applying f instead of its inverse.
why.C: Correct — f and g undo each other, so f(g(5)) = 5, leaving g(5) = (5 + 3)/2 = 4.
why.D: This applies g twice: g(5) = 4, then g(4) = 3.5.

context: The graph of y = f(x) crosses the x-axis only at x = −2 and x = 6. Where does the graph of y = f(2x) cross the x-axis?

why.A: This multiplies the intercepts by 2. A factor inside the function divides the x-values.
why.B: This adds 2 to each intercept, treating f(2x) as a shift.
why.C: This assumes a horizontal stretch leaves the intercepts in place. Only an intercept at 0 would stay put.
why.D: Correct — f(2x) = 0 when 2x = −2 or 2x = 6, so x = −1 or x = 3. The graph is squeezed toward the y-axis.

context: The linear function f(x) = ax + b, with a > 0, satisfies f(f(x)) = 9x + 8 for all x. What is f(2)?

why.A: Correct — f(f(x)) = a²x + ab + b. Then a² = 9 gives a = 3, and 3b + b = 8 gives b = 2, so f(2) = 6 + 2 = 8.
why.B: This is f(f(2)) = 9(2) + 8, applying the given composition instead of f once.
why.C: This takes b = 8 straight from 9x + 8, but the constant term of f(f(x)) is ab + b.
why.D: This solves ab + b = 8 as 2b = 8, treating a as 1 in that term.

context: Which of the following points lies on the line y = 3x − 4?

why.A: This takes the y-intercept as +4. At x = 0 the line is at −4.
why.B: Correct — 3(2) − 4 = 2, which matches the y-coordinate.
why.C: This adds 4 instead of subtracting it: 3(2) + 4 = 10.
why.D: This drops the sign of −2 when multiplying: 3(−2) − 4 is −10, not 2.

context: What is the slope of a line parallel to the line 2x + 5y = 10?

why.A: This drops the negative sign when moving 2x to the other side.
why.B: This takes the reciprocal of the slope. Parallel lines have the same slope, not reciprocal ones.
why.C: Correct — solving for y gives y = −(2/5)x + 2, and parallel lines have equal slopes.
why.D: This reads the coefficient of x without dividing by the coefficient of y.

context: The points (1, 3) and (5, 3) are two adjacent vertices of a square that lies above the segment joining them. Which of the following is another vertex of the square?

why.A: This is 4 units below the segment. The square lies above it.
why.B: This continues along the same horizontal line, which gives a longer segment, not a square.
why.C: This is the center of the square, not a vertex.
why.D: Correct — the side is 4 long, so the square rises 4 units above each of the given vertices, to (1, 7) and (5, 7).

context: A line has slope 3 and passes through the point (2, −1). What is its x-intercept?

why.A: Correct — the line is y + 1 = 3(x − 2), or y = 3x − 7. Setting y = 0 gives x = 7/3.
why.B: This is the y-intercept, the value of y when x = 0.
why.C: This writes the line as y − 1 = 3(x − 2), using +1 for the y-coordinate instead of −1.
why.D: This sets 3x − 7 = 0 but does not divide by 3.

context: What are the coordinates of the centroid of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (9, 0) and (3, 6)?

why.A: This divides the sums by 2 instead of 3, which gives the midpoint of the side from (9, 0) to (3, 6).
why.B: Correct — the centroid averages the three vertices: ((0 + 9 + 3)/3, (0 + 0 + 6)/3) = (4, 2).
why.C: This adds the coordinates without dividing.
why.D: This is the midpoint of the base from (0, 0) to (9, 0), which ignores the third vertex.

context: The point (2, 3) is rotated 90° counterclockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of its image?

why.A: This rotates 90° clockwise, sending (x, y) to (y, −x).
why.B: This reflects across the y-axis, which only changes the sign of x.
why.C: Correct — a 90° counterclockwise rotation sends (x, y) to (−y, x).
why.D: This rotates 180°, changing both signs.

context: The line 2x − 3y = 12 crosses the x-axis at point A and the y-axis at point B. If O is the origin, what is the area of triangle AOB?

why.A: This multiplies the legs without halving.
why.B: This adds the two leg lengths instead of multiplying.
why.C: This is the length of AB, the hypotenuse, not an area.
why.D: Correct — A is (6, 0) and B is (0, −4), so the right triangle AOB has legs 6 and 4 and area ½(6)(4) = 12.

context: At what point does the perpendicular bisector of the segment from (2, 1) to (8, 5) cross the y-axis?

why.A: Correct — the midpoint is (5, 3) and the segment’s slope is 2/3, so the bisector has slope −3/2: y = 3 − (3/2)(x − 5), which gives y = 3 + 15/2 = 21/2 at x = 0.
why.B: This uses the segment’s own slope, 2/3, through the midpoint. That line is not perpendicular to the segment.
why.C: This uses −2/3, changing the sign of the slope without taking the reciprocal.
why.D: This uses the right slope but draws the line through the endpoint (2, 1) instead of the midpoint.

context: What is the area of the triangle bounded by the lines y = x and y = −x + 8 and the x-axis?

why.A: This multiplies base and height without halving.
why.B: Correct — the lines meet at (4, 4), and they cross the x-axis at (0, 0) and (8, 0). The base is 8 and the height is 4, so the area is 16.
why.C: This uses 4, the x-coordinate of the top vertex, as the base.
why.D: This is the height of the triangle, the y-coordinate where the lines meet.

context: Line m has slope −2 and passes through (3, 5). Line n is perpendicular to m and passes through the origin. At what point do lines m and n intersect?

why.A: This gives n slope 2, changing the sign of −2 without taking the reciprocal.
why.B: This gives n slope −1/2, taking the reciprocal without changing the sign.
why.C: Correct — m is y = −2x + 11 and n is y = x/2. Setting x/2 = −2x + 11 gives x = 22/5, and then y = 11/5.
why.D: This writes m as y − 5 = −2(x + 3), with the wrong sign on 3, so m becomes y = −2x − 1.

context: The point (4, −2) is reflected across the line y = 1. What are the coordinates of its image?

why.A: This reflects across the x-axis, y = 0, instead of the line y = 1.
why.B: This reflects across the vertical line x = 1 instead of the horizontal line y = 1.
why.C: This reflects across the line y = x, swapping the coordinates.
why.D: Correct — the point is 3 units below y = 1, so its image is 3 units above it, at y = 4. The x-coordinate does not change.

context: A student has 4 shirts, 3 pairs of pants and 2 pairs of shoes. An outfit is one shirt, one pair of pants and one pair of shoes. How many different outfits are possible?

why.A: Correct — each choice can be paired with every other choice, so the counts multiply: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.
why.B: This adds the numbers of choices instead of multiplying them.
why.C: This pairs shirts with pants but leaves out the choice of shoes.
why.D: This chooses any 3 of the 9 items, which would allow an outfit of three shirts.

context: An integer from 1 through 30 is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is a perfect square?

why.A: This leaves out 1, but 1 = 1² is a perfect square.
why.B: Correct — the perfect squares from 1 to 30 are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25, so the probability is 5/30 = 1/6.
why.C: This counts six squares, adding 36, which is past 30.
why.D: This counts only the even squares, 4 and 16.

context: How many different 3-person committees can be chosen from a group of 7 people?

why.A: This is 7 × 6 × 5, which counts each committee 6 times, once for each order of its members.
why.B: This is 7C2, the number of 2-person committees.
why.C: Correct — order does not matter in a committee, so the count is 7C3 = (7 × 6 × 5)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 35.
why.D: This is 7³, which lets the same person fill more than one seat.

context: A password is 2 letters (A through Z) followed by 3 digits (0 through 9). Letters and digits may repeat. How many different passwords are possible?

why.A: This is 26 × 25 × 10 × 9 × 8, which forbids repeats. The question allows them.
why.B: This adds the choices for each position instead of multiplying.
why.C: This is 36⁵, which lets any position be a letter or a digit.
why.D: Correct — each of the 5 positions is chosen independently: 26 × 26 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 676,000.

context: A team of 3 is chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls. How many different teams have exactly 2 girls?

why.A: Correct — choose the 2 girls in 4C2 = 6 ways and the boy in 5 ways: 6 × 5 = 30.
why.B: This is 9C3, every possible team, whatever its mix of boys and girls.
why.C: This adds the 6 ways to choose the girls and the 5 ways to choose the boy instead of multiplying.
why.D: This chooses the girls in 4 × 3 = 12 ways, counting each pair twice by order.

context: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A or B)?

why.A: This adds the probabilities without subtracting the overlap, counting “both” twice.
why.B: Correct — P(A and B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 for independent events, and P(A or B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.7.
why.C: This is P(A and B), the chance that both happen.
why.D: This is the chance that neither happens, 0.6 × 0.5.

context: A bag holds 3 red, 2 blue and 5 green marbles. A marble is drawn, replaced, and a second marble is drawn. What is the probability that the two marbles are different colors?

why.A: This is the chance of the same color twice, the complement of what is asked.
why.B: This counts each pair of colors in one order only, such as red then blue but not blue then red.
why.C: Correct — the chance of the same color twice is (9 + 4 + 25)/100 = 38/100, so the chance of different colors is 62/100 = 31/50.
why.D: This draws without replacement, but the first marble is put back.

context: Five people, including Ana and Ben, line up in a random order. What is the probability that Ana is first in line and Ben is last?

why.A: This multiplies 1/5 by 1/5, as if Ben could also be in Ana’s place.
why.B: This counts Ana and Ben at the two ends in either order. The question fixes who is first.
why.C: This adds the two probabilities instead of multiplying them.
why.D: Correct — Ana is first with probability 1/5, and then Ben is last with probability 1/4 among the 4 remaining places: 1/5 × 1/4 = 1/20.

context: A box holds 20 light bulbs, 4 of which are defective. Three bulbs are chosen at random without replacement. What is the probability that at least one of them is defective?

why.A: Correct — the chance that none is defective is 16C3/20C3 = 560/1,140 = 28/57, so at least one is 1 − 28/57 = 29/57.
why.B: This is the chance that none of the three is defective, the complement.
why.C: This adds 4/20 three times. Adding counts the overlaps, where two or three are defective, more than once.
why.D: This computes 1 − (4/5)³, which replaces each bulb before the next draw.

context: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled, and the sum is 8. Given this, what is the probability that one of the dice shows a 3?

why.A: This is 2/36, the chance of a sum of 8 with a 3 before the condition is applied.
why.B: Correct — a sum of 8 comes from (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3) and (6, 2). Two of these five outcomes include a 3.
why.C: This is the chance of rolling at least one 3, ignoring that the sum is known to be 8.
why.D: This lists the pairs without order, {2, 6}, {3, 5} and {4, 4}, but those three are not equally likely.

context: How many different arrangements of the letters in the word LEVEL are possible?

why.A: This treats all five letters as different.
why.B: This allows for only one repeated letter. Both L and E repeat.
why.C: Correct — 5 letters give 5! = 120 orders, but swapping the two L’s or the two E’s gives the same word, so 120 ÷ (2 × 2) = 30.
why.D: This arranges only the three distinct letters, L, E and V.

context: A sequence is defined by aₙ = 3n − 5. What is the 6th term?

why.A: This is a₅, one term too early.
why.B: This computes 3(6) and leaves out the − 5.
why.C: This subtracts in the wrong order, 5 − 18.
why.D: Correct — a₆ = 3(6) − 5 = 13.

context: What is the common ratio of the geometric sequence 81, 27, 9, …?

why.A: Correct — each term is the one before it divided by 3, which is multiplying by 1/3: 27/81 = 1/3.
why.B: This divides each term by the next. The ratio is a later term over the earlier one.
why.C: This is the difference 27 − 81, which describes an arithmetic sequence.
why.D: This divides the third term by the first, 9/81, which spans two steps.

context: A savings jar starts with $15, and $4 is added at the end of each week. How many dollars are in the jar after 10 weeks?

why.A: This counts only 9 additions, as if the first week added nothing.
why.B: Correct — 10 weekly additions of $4 add $40 to the starting $15.
why.C: This counts the additions but forgets the $15 already in the jar.
why.D: This counts 11 additions for 10 weeks.

context: In the geometric sequence 2, 6, 18, …, which term is equal to 1,458?

why.A: This stops at the exponent in 3⁶ = 729. The exponent is n − 1, not n.
why.B: This divides 1,458 by the second term, 6, which gives no term number.
why.C: Correct — the nth term is 2(3ⁿ⁻¹). Then 3ⁿ⁻¹ = 729 = 3⁶, so n − 1 = 6 and n = 7.
why.D: This is 1,458 ÷ 2, the value of 3ⁿ⁻¹, not the term number.

context: In an arithmetic sequence, the 1st term is 8 and the 5th term is 20. What is the sum of the first 5 terms?

why.A: This multiplies 5 by 8 + 20 without halving to get the average term.
why.B: This adds only the first and last terms.
why.C: This uses 4 terms, counting the steps between the 1st and 5th terms instead of the terms.
why.D: Correct — the sum is the number of terms times the average of the first and last: 5 × (8 + 20)/2 = 70. (The terms are 8, 11, 14, 17, 20.)

context: A ball is dropped from a height of 81 feet. Each time it bounces, it rises to 2/3 of the height of its previous fall. How high, in feet, does it rise after the 3rd bounce?

why.A: Correct — after 3 bounces the height is 81 × (2/3)³ = 81 × 8/27 = 24.
why.B: This is the height after the 2nd bounce, 81 × (2/3)².
why.C: This is the height after the 4th bounce.
why.D: This multiplies by 1/3 each time, the fraction of height lost rather than kept.

context: A sequence is defined by a₁ = 1 and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + n for n ≥ 2. What is a₅?

why.A: This is a₄, one step short.
why.C: This adds 2 every time, as if the sequence were arithmetic. The amount added grows with n.
why.D: This is a₆, one step too far.

context: What is the sum of the geometric series 3 + 6 + 12 + … + 384?

why.A: This uses 3 × 2⁸, leaving out the − 1 in the sum formula.
why.B: This counts 7 terms, reading the exponent in 384 = 3 × 2⁷ as the number of terms. The exponents run from 0 to 7, which is 8 terms.
why.C: Correct — 384 = 3 × 2⁷, so there are 8 terms, and the sum is 3(2⁸ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 765.
why.D: This uses the arithmetic-series rule, 8 × (3 + 384)/2. Averaging the ends works only when the terms grow by a constant difference.

context: The first three terms of an arithmetic sequence are x, 2x + 1 and 5x − 2. What is the 4th term?

why.A: This is x, the first term, not the 4th.
why.B: This is the 5th term, one step too far.
why.C: This is the common difference, 5 − 2.
why.D: Correct — the middle term is the average of its neighbors, so 2(2x + 1) = x + (5x − 2), giving x = 2. The terms are 2, 5, 8, so the 4th is 11.

context: In a geometric sequence with positive terms, the 2nd term is 6 and the 4th term is 54. What is the 7th term?

why.A: Correct — two steps multiply by r² = 54/6 = 9, so r = 3. Three more steps give 54 × 3³ = 1,458.
why.B: This takes 54/6 = 9 as the ratio, but the 2nd and 4th terms are two steps apart, so 9 is r².
why.C: This treats the sequence as arithmetic, adding (54 − 6)/2 = 24 each step.
why.D: This is the 6th term, one step short.

context: A sequence is defined by aₙ = (−1)ⁿ · n. What is the sum of the first 100 terms?

why.A: This assumes the signs make everything cancel. Each pair leaves 1, because the positive term is always larger.
why.B: Correct — the terms pair up as (−1 + 2) + (−3 + 4) + … + (−99 + 100), which is 50 pairs of 1.
why.C: This starts with a positive term. With n = 1, (−1)¹ makes the first term −1.
why.D: This ignores the alternating signs and adds 1 through 100.

context: A circular garden has a diameter of 12 meters. Using π ≈ 3.14, about how many meters of fencing are needed to go around it?

why.A: This uses 12 as the radius, computing 2π(12).
why.B: This is the area, π(6²), not the distance around.
why.C: Correct — the circumference is π times the diameter: 3.14 × 12 = 37.68.
why.D: This multiplies π by the radius, 6, which is half the circumference.

context: A circle has the equation x² + y² = 49. What is its diameter?

why.A: This is the radius.
why.B: This reads r² as the radius.
why.C: This halves 49 instead of taking its square root.
why.D: Correct — the equation says r² = 49, so r = 7 and the diameter is 14.

context: A window is shaped like a semicircle with a diameter of 10 feet. What is the perimeter of the window, including the straight edge?

why.A: Correct — the curved edge is half of π(10) = 10π, which is 5π, and the straight edge is the 10-foot diameter.
why.B: This counts only the curved edge and leaves out the straight edge.
why.C: This uses the full circumference for the curved edge.
why.D: This is the area of the semicircle, ½π(5²), not its perimeter.

context: Chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at point E. If AE = 4, EB = 9 and CE = 6, what is ED?

why.A: This pairs the segments wrongly, solving 4 × ED = 6 × 9.
why.B: Correct — the products of the segments of intersecting chords are equal: 4 × 9 = 6 × ED, so ED = 6.
why.C: This pairs the segments wrongly, solving 9 × ED = 4 × 6.
why.D: This sets the sums equal: 4 + 9 = 6 + ED. Equal chords would have equal sums, but these chords need not be equal.

context: Which equation describes the circle with center (−1, 2) that passes through the origin?

why.A: This keeps the center’s signs inside the parentheses. The form (x − h)² needs h = −1, which gives x + 1.
why.B: This puts the radius on the right side. The equation uses r², which is 5.
why.C: Correct — the radius is the distance to (0, 0): r² = 1² + 2² = 5.
why.D: This adds 1 and 4 to get 5 and then squares it, squaring the radius twice.

context: A sector of a circle has a central angle of 45° and an area of 8π. What is the radius of the circle?

why.A: This is r², the step before taking the square root.
why.B: This uses the arc-length formula, (1/8)(2πr) = 8π, instead of the area formula.
why.C: This treats 8π as the area of the whole circle, forgetting that the sector is 1/8 of it.
why.D: Correct — the sector is 45/360 = 1/8 of the circle, so the whole circle has area 64π, and r² = 64.

context: A wheel with a diameter of 28 inches rolls in a straight line for 440 feet without slipping. Using π ≈ 22/7, how many complete turns does the wheel make?

why.A: Correct — one turn covers (22/7)(28) = 88 inches, and 440 feet is 5,280 inches, so the wheel turns 5,280 ÷ 88 = 60 times.
why.B: This divides 440 by 88 without converting feet to inches.
why.C: This uses π times the radius, 44 inches, as the distance for one turn.
why.D: This uses 2π times the diameter, 176 inches, doubling the circumference.

context: From a point P outside a circle, two tangent segments touch the circle at A and B. Angle APB measures 50°. What is the measure of minor arc AB?

why.A: This takes the arc to equal the angle at P. The angle at P and the central angle are supplementary, not equal.
why.B: Correct — each radius meets its tangent at 90°, so in quadrilateral PAOB the central angle AOB is 360° − 90° − 90° − 50° = 130°, and the minor arc matches it.
why.C: This doubles the angle at P, as if it were an inscribed angle. P is outside the circle.
why.D: This is the major arc, 360° − 130°.

context: The equation x² + y² + 4x − 10y = k describes a circle with radius 6. What is the value of k?

why.A: This sets k equal to r² without completing the square.
why.B: This adds 29 to 36 instead of subtracting it.
why.C: Correct — completing the square gives (x + 2)² + (y − 5)² = k + 4 + 25. The right side must be 6² = 36, so k = 7.
why.D: This subtracts 4 and 10, the coefficients themselves, instead of the squares of their halves, 4 and 25.

context: A square is inscribed in a circle, and the circle is inscribed in a larger square. What is the ratio of the area of the smaller square to the area of the larger square?

why.A: This is the ratio of the side lengths. Areas scale by the square of that ratio.
why.B: This compares the circle to the larger square instead of comparing the two squares.
why.C: This compares the smaller square to the circle.
why.D: Correct — with circle radius r, the larger square has side 2r and area 4r². The smaller square’s diagonal is 2r, so its area is (2r)²/2 = 2r².

context: In a circle with center O and radius 10, chord AB subtends a central angle of 120°. What is the length of chord AB?

why.A: Correct — the perpendicular from O bisects AB and the 120° angle, making a 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse 10. Half the chord is 5√3, so AB = 10√3.
why.B: This treats triangle AOB as equilateral, which needs a 60° central angle.
why.C: This is the length of arc AB, (120/360)(20π), not the straight chord.
why.D: This is half the chord, from A to the foot of the perpendicular.

context: A farm has only chickens and cows. Together the animals have 20 heads and 56 legs. How many cows are on the farm?

why.A: This is the number of chickens, 20 − 8.
why.B: Correct — with c chickens and w cows, c + w = 20 and 2c + 4w = 56. Subtracting twice the first equation leaves 2w = 16.
why.C: This divides the 56 legs by 4, as if every animal were a cow.
why.D: This subtracts only 1 leg per head, (56 − 20) ÷ 2. Every animal has at least 2 legs, so 2 × 20 = 40 must come off first.

context: Which ordered pair (x, y) satisfies both 3x + y = 5 and x − y = 3?

why.A: This finds x = 2 but drops the sign when solving 2 − y = 3 for y.
why.B: This satisfies 3x + y = 5 but not x − y = 3, since 1 − 2 = −1.
why.C: Correct — adding the equations gives 4x = 8, so x = 2, and then 2 − y = 3 gives y = −1. Check: 3(2) + (−1) = 5.
why.D: This satisfies x − y = 3 but not 3x + y = 5, since 3(3) + 0 = 9.

context: In the xy-plane, the graphs of y = 4 and y = 2x − 6 intersect at a point. What is the x-coordinate of that point?

why.A: This is the y-coordinate of the intersection, not the x-coordinate.
why.B: This divides 4 by 2 and leaves out the − 6.
why.C: This subtracts 6 from 4 instead of adding 6 to both sides.
why.D: Correct — at the intersection both equations give the same y, so 2x − 6 = 4, 2x = 10 and x = 5.

context: The larger of two numbers is 3 more than twice the smaller, and the sum of the two numbers is 39. What is the larger number?

why.A: Correct — with smaller number s, s + (2s + 3) = 39, so 3s = 36, s = 12 and the larger is 2(12) + 3 = 27.
why.B: This is the smaller number. The question asks for the larger.
why.C: This divides 39 by 3 without first removing the extra 3.
why.D: This writes the larger number as 2s − 3, reading “3 more than” as 3 less.

context: If 3x + 4y = 10 and 2x + 3y = 7, what is the value of x + y?

why.A: This adds the equations, which gives 5x + 7y = 17, not x + y.
why.B: Correct — subtracting the second equation from the first gives x + y = 10 − 7 = 3 in one step. (Solving fully gives x = 2 and y = 1.)
why.C: This is the value of x alone.
why.D: This is the value of y alone.

context: Rental shop A charges $30 plus $5 per hour. Rental shop B charges $12 plus $8 per hour. For how many hours of rental do the two shops charge the same amount?

why.A: This is the equal cost, 30 + 5(6), not the number of hours.
why.B: This divides the $18 difference in fees by shop A’s $5 rate instead of by the $3 difference in rates.
why.C: Correct — setting 30 + 5h = 12 + 8h gives 18 = 3h, so h = 6.
why.D: This adds the two fees and divides by 3, treating the fees as if they combined.

context: If y = x/2 + 1 and 3x − 2y = 10, what is the value of y?

why.A: This is the value of x.
why.B: This multiplies only x/2 by 2 and not the + 1, getting 2x − 1 = 10 and x = 5.5.
why.C: This is x − y, not y.
why.D: Correct — substituting gives 3x − 2(x/2 + 1) = 10, so 3x − x − 2 = 10, x = 6 and y = 6/2 + 1 = 4.

context: The system y = 2x + 3 and y = ax − 1 has no solution. What is the value of a?

why.A: Correct — two lines with different y-intercepts never meet when they are parallel, so their slopes must match: a = 2.
why.B: This makes the slopes opposites. Lines with slopes 2 and −2 cross.
why.C: This makes the lines perpendicular, which guarantees they cross.
why.D: This matches the y-intercepts. Equal intercepts give a shared point, not no solution.

context: A chemist mixes a 10% salt solution with a 40% salt solution to make 30 liters of a 20% salt solution. How many liters of the 40% solution are used?

why.A: This is the amount of the 10% solution. The 20% target is closer to 10%, so more of the weaker solution is needed.
why.B: Correct — with b liters of 40%, 0.10(30 − b) + 0.40b = 0.20(30). Then 3 + 0.3b = 6, so b = 10.
why.C: This splits the 30 liters evenly, which would give a 25% mixture.
why.D: This is the number of liters of salt in the final mixture, 0.20 × 30.

context: The system ax + 3y = 10 and 4x + by = 20 has infinitely many solutions. What is the value of a + b?

why.A: This takes the first equation as twice the second, giving a = 8 and b = 1.5. The constants show that 20 is twice 10, not the reverse.
why.B: This copies the coefficients across, a = 4 and b = 3, without scaling by the factor of 2.
why.C: Correct — the second equation must be exactly twice the first, since 20 = 2 × 10. So 4 = 2a and b = 2 × 3, giving a = 2 and b = 6.
why.D: This is the product ab, 2 × 6, not the sum.

context: If 1/x + 1/y = 5 and 1/x − 1/y = 1, what is the value of x?

why.A: This is the value of 1/x. The last step is to take its reciprocal.
why.B: This is the value of y, since 2/y = 4 gives y = 1/2.
why.C: This is the value of 1/y.
why.D: Correct — adding the equations gives 2/x = 6, so 1/x = 3 and x = 1/3.

context: The graphs of y = x² − 3 and y = x + 3 intersect at two points. What is the sum of the y-coordinates of those two points?

why.A: Correct — setting x² − 3 = x + 3 gives x² − x − 6 = 0, so x = 3 or x = −2. The points are (3, 6) and (−2, 1), and 6 + 1 = 7.
why.B: This is the sum of the x-coordinates, 3 + (−2).
why.C: This factors x² − x − 6 as (x + 3)(x − 2), giving x = −3 and 2 and the points (−3, 0) and (2, 5).
why.D: This is the product of the x-coordinates, the constant term of x² − x − 6.

context: The value of log₂ 10 lies between which two consecutive integers?

why.A: This takes 2⁴ = 16 as the power just below 10. It is already above 10.
why.B: Correct — 2³ = 8 and 2⁴ = 16, and 10 lies between 8 and 16, so the exponent lies between 3 and 4.
why.C: This treats the logarithm as base 10, where log 10 = 1.
why.D: This divides 10 by 2, treating the logarithm as division.

context: What is the value of 10^(log 7), where log means the logarithm base 10?

why.A: This treats log 7 as if it were 7 itself.
why.B: This multiplies 10 by 7 instead of using 10 as the base of a power.
why.C: Correct — log 7 is the exponent that turns 10 into 7, so raising 10 to that exponent gives back 7.
why.D: This cancels 10 against log as if they divided out, leaving nothing behind.

context: What is the value of log₃(3⁵ · 3²)?

why.A: This multiplies the exponents. Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents.
why.B: This is 3⁷ itself, the number inside the logarithm, not the logarithm.
why.C: This takes the logarithm of 3⁵ and drops the second factor.
why.D: Correct — 3⁵ · 3² = 3⁷, and log₃(3⁷) = 7.

context: If log₃(2x + 1) = 2, what is the value of x?

why.A: Correct — rewriting in exponential form gives 2x + 1 = 3² = 9, so x = 4.
why.B: This finds 2x + 1 = 9 but subtracts 1 and stops, forgetting to divide by 2.
why.C: This drops the logarithm and sets 2x + 1 = 2.
why.D: This swaps the base and exponent, getting 2x + 1 = 2³ = 8.

context: Which expression is equal to 2 log x − log y?

why.A: This multiplies x by the coefficient 2. A coefficient on a logarithm becomes an exponent.
why.B: Correct — 2 log x = log(x²), and subtracting a logarithm divides: log(x²) − log y = log(x²/y).
why.C: This turns the difference of logarithms into the logarithm of a difference. It becomes the logarithm of a quotient.
why.D: This applies the 2 to y as well, but only log x is doubled.

context: The pH of a solution is −log[H⁺], where [H⁺] is its hydrogen-ion concentration. Solution A has 100 times the hydrogen-ion concentration of solution B. How does the pH of solution A compare with the pH of solution B?

why.A: This ignores the minus sign in the formula. A higher concentration gives a lower pH.
why.B: This uses the ratio of concentrations directly. The logarithm turns a factor of 100 into a change of 2.
why.C: Correct — log(100[H⁺]) = 2 + log[H⁺], and the minus sign in the pH formula turns that into a pH 2 lower.
why.D: This treats pH as inversely proportional to concentration. The logarithm makes the change a fixed subtraction.

context: If logₓ 81 = 4, where x > 0, what is the value of x?

why.A: This takes the square root of 81. The equation needs the fourth root.
why.B: This divides 81 by 4, treating the logarithm as division.
why.C: This multiplies 81 by 4 instead of taking a root.
why.D: Correct — logₓ 81 = 4 means x⁴ = 81, and 3⁴ = 81.

context: If log₂ x = 3 and log₂ y = 5, what is the value of log₄(xy)?

why.A: Correct — log₂(xy) = 3 + 5 = 8, and since 4 = 2², log₄(xy) = 8/2 = 4. (xy = 2⁸ = 4⁴.)
why.B: This is log₂(xy). It still has to be converted to base 4.
why.C: This multiplies by 2 when changing to base 4. A larger base gives a smaller logarithm.
why.D: This multiplies the logarithms, 3 × 5 = 15, before halving. The logarithm of a product is a sum.

context: An account grows by 8% each year. Which expression gives the number of years it takes for the balance to double?

why.A: This uses the growth rate 0.08 as the base. Each year the balance is multiplied by 1.08.
why.B: Correct — doubling means 1.08ᵗ = 2, and taking the logarithm of both sides gives t log 1.08 = log 2.
why.C: This inverts the quotient when dividing both sides by log 1.08.
why.D: This turns t log 1.08 = log 2 into a single logarithm of a quotient, which is not the same as dividing logarithms.

context: If log₃ 5 = a, what is the value of 9^(a + 1)?

why.A: This treats 9ᵃ as 5. Changing the base from 3 to 9 squares the value.
why.B: This multiplies 25 by 3 instead of by 9 for the extra power.
why.D: This adds 1 to 9ᵃ instead of multiplying by 9¹.

context: On a certain earthquake scale, each increase of 1 in magnitude means the ground motion is 10 times as large. About how many times as large is the ground motion of a magnitude 7.2 earthquake as that of a magnitude 5.7 earthquake?

why.A: This multiplies 10 by the difference of 1.5 instead of raising 10 to that power.
why.B: This is the difference in magnitude, not the ratio of ground motion.
why.C: This divides the magnitudes, 7.2 ÷ 5.7. The scale is logarithmic, so the difference is what counts.
why.D: Correct — the magnitudes differ by 1.5, so the ratio is 10^1.5 = 10√10 ≈ 31.6.

context: What is the sum of the entries on the main diagonal (top left to bottom right) of the matrix [[5, −2], [7, 3]]?

why.A: Correct — the main diagonal holds 5 and 3, and 5 + 3 = 8.
why.B: This adds the other diagonal, −2 + 7.
why.C: This adds all four entries.
why.D: This multiplies the diagonal entries instead of adding them.

why.A: This subtracts 1 and 3 from the result instead of adding them, getting a = 4 and b = 3.
why.B: Correct — matching entries gives a − 1 = 5 and b − 3 = 6, so a = 6, b = 9 and a + b = 15.
why.C: This adds the entries of the result, 5 + 6, which are the differences, not a and b.
why.D: This is the product ab, 6 × 9, not the sum.

context: Matrices P and Q both have 3 rows and 4 columns. Which of the following describes the product PQ?

why.A: This keeps the common shape, which is the rule for adding matrices, not multiplying them.
why.B: This pairs the row counts of the two matrices. The product takes P’s rows and Q’s columns, and only when P’s columns match Q’s rows.
why.C: Correct — PQ needs the 4 columns of P to match the rows of Q, and Q has only 3 rows.
why.D: This pairs the column counts of the two matrices, which is the shape of a product of a 4 × 3 matrix and a 3 × 4 matrix.

why.A: This is AB. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so the order matters.
why.B: This multiplies matching entries, which is not how matrix products work.
why.C: This is A + B.
why.D: Correct — BA takes rows of B times columns of A: row 2 of B gives 4(2) + 2(0) = 8 and 4(1) + 2(3) = 10.

context: What is the inverse of the matrix [[2, 0], [0, 5]]?

why.A: Correct — for a diagonal matrix, the inverse takes the reciprocal of each diagonal entry. Check: 2 × 1/2 = 1 and 5 × 1/5 = 1.
why.B: This swaps the diagonal entries, the first step of the 2 × 2 formula, but skips dividing by the determinant, 10.
why.C: This negates the entries, which gives the additive inverse, not the multiplicative inverse.
why.D: This takes reciprocals but also swaps them, so the product has 2/5 and 5/2 on the diagonal.

context: Matrix A has dimensions 2 × 3, and matrix B has dimensions 2 × 2. Which of the products AB and BA is defined?

why.A: This checks the rows of the first matrix against the rows of the second. The columns of the first must match the rows of the second.
why.B: Correct — BA is (2 × 2)(2 × 3), and B’s 2 columns match A’s 2 rows. AB is (2 × 3)(2 × 2), where 3 columns do not match 2 rows.
why.C: This assumes any two matrices with a shared dimension can be multiplied in either order.
why.D: This expects the matrices to be the same size. B’s 2 columns do match A’s 2 rows.

why.A: This is x + y, not xy.
why.B: This forgets to divide by 2, taking x = 6 and y = 10.
why.C: Correct — the top-left entries give 2x + 1 = 7, so x = 3, and the bottom-right give 2y − 2 = 8, so y = 5.
why.D: This subtracts 2 from 8 instead of adding it, getting 2y = 6 and y = 3.

context: If A = [[0, 1], [1, 0]], what is A⁵⁰?

why.A: This raises each entry to the 50th power. Matrix powers are repeated matrix products.
why.B: This multiplies each entry by 50, treating the power as a scalar multiple.
why.C: This finds that A² is the identity but then multiplies it by 50 instead of raising it to the 25th power.
why.D: Correct — A² is the identity matrix, so A⁵⁰ = (A²)²⁵ is the identity too.

context: If A = [[2, 1], [1, 1]] and AX = [[5, 2], [3, 1]], what is matrix X?

why.B: This multiplies by A⁻¹ on the right. Since A is on the left of X, A⁻¹ must go on the left.
why.C: This divides entry by entry, which is not how to undo a matrix product.
why.D: This subtracts A from the result, treating the product as a sum.

context: If A = [[1, k], [0, 1]] and A² = [[1, 6], [0, 1]], what is the value of k?

why.A: This squares each entry, setting k² = 6. Matrix squaring is a matrix product.
why.B: Correct — multiplying gives A² = [[1, 2k], [0, 1]], so 2k = 6 and k = 3.
why.C: This assumes squaring leaves the corner entry unchanged.
why.D: This doubles 6 instead of halving it.

context: The matrix [[3, 2], [4, x]] has an inverse, and the top-left entry of that inverse is 1. What is the value of x?

why.A: This uses the original top-left entry, setting 3/(3x − 8) = 1. The formula swaps the diagonal entries.
why.B: This computes the determinant as 8 − 3x, reversing the order of the products.
why.C: Correct — the inverse’s top-left entry is x/(3x − 8). Setting x/(3x − 8) = 1 gives x = 3x − 8, so x = 4.
why.D: This sets x itself equal to 1, forgetting to divide by the determinant.

context: What is 4i − (3 − 2i)?

why.A: This changes the sign of −2i but not of the 3.
why.B: This changes the sign of the 3 but subtracts 2i instead of adding it.
why.C: This treats 3 as if it were 3i, combining 4i − 3i + 2i.
why.D: Correct — distributing the minus sign gives 4i − 3 + 2i = −3 + 6i.

context: For what real value of b is (2 + bi) + (3 − 4i) a real number?

why.A: Correct — the imaginary part is (b − 4)i, which is 0 only when b = 4.
why.B: This sets b + 4 = 0, forgetting that 4i is being subtracted.
why.C: This is the real part of the sum, 2 + 3.
why.D: This makes the first number real, but the second number’s −4i would remain.

context: What is (2 + i)(2 − i)(1 + i)?

why.A: This takes i² as 1, so (2 + i)(2 − i) becomes 4 − 1 = 3.
why.C: This multiplies only the real part of 1 + i by 5.
why.D: This multiplies only the first terms, 2 × 2 = 4, and drops the −i² term.

context: What is |(3 + 4i)(1 − i)|?

why.A: This adds the absolute values, 5 and √2. The absolute value of a product is their product.
why.B: This is the real part of the product, 7 + i.
why.C: Correct — the product is 3 − 3i + 4i − 4i² = 7 + i, and |7 + i| = √(49 + 1) = √50 = 5√2.
why.D: This is 7² + 1² without the square root.

context: What is the complex conjugate of (2 + i)²?

why.A: This is (2 + i)² itself, before taking the conjugate.
why.B: This takes i² as 1, getting 5 + 4i before conjugating.
why.C: This negates both parts, which gives the opposite, not the conjugate.
why.D: Correct — (2 + i)² = 4 + 4i + i² = 3 + 4i, and its conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part.

context: For real numbers x and y, (x + yi) − (4 − 3i) = 2x + 5i. What is the value of x + y?

why.A: Correct — the real parts give x − 4 = 2x, so x = −4. The imaginary parts give y + 3 = 5, so y = 2.
why.B: This takes the imaginary part as y − 3, missing that subtracting −3i adds 3i, and gets y = 8.
why.C: This solves x − 4 = 2x as x = 4, dropping the sign.
why.D: This is the product xy, not the sum.

context: What is the value of i + i² + i³ + … + i¹⁰³?

why.A: This assumes all the terms cancel, but 103 is not a multiple of 4, so three terms are left.
why.B: Correct — each group of four powers adds to 0, so the first 100 terms cancel. The last three are i¹⁰¹ + i¹⁰² + i¹⁰³ = i − 1 − i = −1.
why.C: This keeps only i¹⁰¹ from the leftover terms.
why.D: This keeps only i¹⁰³ from the leftover terms.

context: If z = 1 + 2i and z̄ is its complex conjugate, what is z/z̄?

why.A: This treats z̄ as −z. Taking the conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part only.
why.B: This takes i² as 1, so (1 + 2i)² becomes 5 + 4i.
why.C: Correct — multiplying top and bottom by 1 + 2i gives (1 + 2i)²/(1 + 4) = (−3 + 4i)/5.
why.D: This computes the denominator as 1 − 4 = −3, taking (1 − 2i)(1 + 2i) as 1 − 4 instead of 1 − 4i².

context: One solution of x² + bx + c = 0, where b and c are real numbers, is 3 − 2i. What is the value of c?

why.A: This takes the product as 9 − 4, using i² = 1.
why.B: This is b, the negative of the sum of the roots.
why.C: This is the sum of the roots, which equals −b, not c.
why.D: Correct — the other root is the conjugate 3 + 2i, and c is the product of the roots: (3 − 2i)(3 + 2i) = 9 + 4 = 13.

context: For what real value of k is (k + 2i)(1 − 3i) a real number?

why.A: Correct — the product is (k + 6) + (2 − 3k)i, which is real when 2 − 3k = 0.
why.B: This takes the imaginary part as 2 + 3k, missing that −3i times k gives −3k.
why.C: This solves 2 − 3k = 0 as k = 3/2, dividing the wrong way.
why.D: This sets the real part k + 6 to 0, which makes the product purely imaginary instead of real.

context: A restaurant bill is $24, and the diner adds an 18% tip. What is the total, including the tip?

why.A: This is the tip alone. The question asks for the bill plus the tip.
why.C: This adds 18 dollars instead of 18 percent.
why.D: This subtracts the tip from the bill instead of adding it.

context: Which fraction is equal to 0.45?

why.A: This places the two digits over each other. 0.45 means 45 hundredths.
why.B: This reads 0.45 as 45/10, one place value off, and simplifies that to 9/2.
why.C: Correct — 0.45 = 45/100, and dividing the top and bottom by 5 gives 9/20.
why.D: This reads 0.45 as 45 thousandths, one place value too small.

context: After a 30% discount, a bicycle costs $168. What was the price before the discount?

why.A: This adds 30% of $168 back on. The discount was 30% of the original, larger price.
why.B: This takes another 30% off the sale price.
why.C: This divides by 0.30, the discount, instead of by 0.70, the part that is paid.
why.D: Correct — the sale price is 70% of the original, so the original is 168 ÷ 0.70 = $240.

context: What is 2¼ × 1⅓?

why.A: Correct — as improper fractions, 9/4 × 4/3 = 36/12 = 3.
why.B: This multiplies the whole parts and the fraction parts separately, 2 × 1 and 1/4 × 1/3.
why.C: This adds the two numbers instead of multiplying them.
why.D: This multiplies only the whole-number parts, 2 × 1, and drops the fractions.

context: The ratio of red marbles to blue marbles in a jar is 3 : 5, and there are 12 more blue marbles than red marbles. How many marbles are in the jar?

why.A: This is the number of red marbles, 3 × 6.
why.B: Correct — blue exceeds red by 5 − 3 = 2 parts, so 2 parts = 12 and 1 part = 6. The jar holds 8 parts, or 48 marbles.
why.C: This is the number of blue marbles, 5 × 6.
why.D: This treats the 12 extra marbles as one part instead of two, getting 8 × 12.

context: A 2-pound bag of trail mix contains 12 ounces of nuts. What percent of the bag’s weight is nuts? (1 pound = 16 ounces)

why.A: This compares 12 ounces with 1 pound, 16 ounces, and forgets that the bag weighs 2 pounds.
why.B: This converts 2 pounds to 20 ounces, using 10 ounces per pound.
why.C: Correct — 2 pounds is 32 ounces, and 12/32 = 0.375, or 37.5%.
why.D: This is the percent of the bag that is not nuts, 20/32.

context: A stock’s price rises 10% in each of two years and then falls 20% in the third year. What is the net change in price over the three years?

why.A: This adds the percents, 10 + 10 − 20 = 0. Each change applies to a different base.
why.B: This compounds the two rises to 21% but then subtracts 20 points instead of taking 20% of the new price.
why.C: This reads the multiplier 0.968 as the size of the change. A multiplier of 0.968 means 96.8% of the price remains.
why.D: Correct — the price is multiplied by 1.1 × 1.1 × 0.8 = 0.968, which is 3.2% below the start.

context: At a school, 3/5 of the students take Spanish, 1/4 take French, and 1/10 take both. What fraction of the students take neither language?

why.A: Correct — the fraction taking at least one is 3/5 + 1/4 − 1/10 = 12/20 + 5/20 − 2/20 = 15/20, so 5/20 = 1/4 take neither.
why.B: This adds 3/5 and 1/4 without removing the students counted twice.
why.C: This subtracts the students who take both a second time, removing them from the total twice.
why.D: This is the fraction who take at least one language.

context: Jo spent 1/3 of her money on a book and then 1/4 of what was left on lunch. She had $30 left. How much money did she start with?

why.A: This takes lunch as 1/4 of the original amount, so she keeps 1 − 1/3 − 1/4 = 5/12 of it.
why.B: Correct — after the book she had 2/3 of her money, and after lunch 3/4 of that, so (3/4)(2/3)x = x/2 = 30.
why.C: This undoes the lunch step only, 30 ÷ 3/4, and stops before undoing the book.
why.D: This undoes the book step only, 30 ÷ 2/3, and skips the lunch step.

context: If 3(x + 2) = 21, what is the value of x + 2?

why.A: This is the value of x. The question asks for x + 2.
why.B: This subtracts 2 from 21 without first dividing by 3.
why.C: Correct — dividing both sides by 3 gives x + 2 = 7 directly.
why.D: This multiplies 21 by 3 instead of dividing.

context: If x/4 − 3 = 2, what is the value of x?

why.A: This subtracts 3 instead of adding it, getting x/4 = −1.
why.B: This divides 5 by 4 at the last step instead of multiplying.
why.C: This multiplies 2 by 4 and then adds 3, undoing the steps in the wrong order.
why.D: Correct — adding 3 gives x/4 = 5, and multiplying by 4 gives x = 20.

context: What value of x satisfies 0.2x = 0.05x + 3?

why.A: Correct — subtracting 0.05x gives 0.15x = 3, so x = 3 ÷ 0.15 = 20.
why.B: This adds 0.05x to 0.2x, getting 0.25x = 3.
why.C: This multiplies 3 by 0.15 instead of dividing.
why.D: This divides 3 by 0.2, ignoring the 0.05x term.

context: For what value of c is 4(x − c) = 4x − 12 true for every value of x?

why.A: This drops the sign, setting −4c equal to +12.
why.B: Correct — the left side is 4x − 4c, which matches 4x − 12 for every x when 4c = 12.
why.C: This matches c to 12 without distributing the 4 to c.
why.D: This multiplies 12 by 4 instead of dividing.

context: Ana is 4 times as old as her son. In 20 years, she will be twice as old as her son. How old is her son now?

why.A: This is Ana’s age now, 4 × 10.
why.B: This adds 20 years to the son’s age but not to Ana’s, solving 4s = 2(s + 20).
why.C: Correct — with son’s age s, 4s + 20 = 2(s + 20). Then 4s + 20 = 2s + 40, so s = 10.
why.D: This is the son’s age in 20 years.

context: The formula A = P + Prt gives the value of a simple-interest account. Which equation gives r in terms of A, P and t?

why.A: This divides every term by Pt but simplifies P/(Pt) to 1 instead of 1/t.
why.B: This multiplies by t instead of dividing by it.
why.C: This subtracts Pt instead of dividing by it.
why.D: Correct — subtracting P gives A − P = Prt, and dividing by Pt isolates r.

context: The equation 2(3x − 4) = ax + b has infinitely many solutions. What is the value of a + b?

why.A: Correct — the left side is 6x − 8, and infinitely many solutions means the sides are identical: a = 6 and b = −8.
why.B: This distributes the 2 to 3x but not to −4, getting b = −4.
why.C: This drops the sign on the constant, taking b = 8.
why.D: This is the product ab, not the sum.

context: The total cost of a phone was $231, which included 8% sales tax on the phone’s price and a $15 shipping fee that is not taxed. What was the phone’s price before tax?

why.A: This removes the shipping fee but not the tax.
why.C: This takes 8% off $216. The tax was 8% of the smaller price, so the step is dividing by 1.08.
why.D: This divides the whole total by 1.08 before removing the shipping, so the untaxed fee is treated as taxed.

context: If 2/(x − 1) = 3/(x + 2), what is the value of x?

why.A: This multiplies only the x-terms when cross-multiplying, getting 2x + 2 = 3x − 1.
why.B: This pairs each numerator with its own denominator, 2(x − 1) = 3(x + 2).
why.C: Correct — cross-multiplying gives 2(x + 2) = 3(x − 1), so 2x + 4 = 3x − 3 and x = 7.
why.D: This solves −x = −7 as x = −7, losing the sign in the last step.

context: The sum of three consecutive even integers is 150 more than the smallest of them. What is the largest of the three integers?

why.A: This is the smallest of the three integers.
why.B: This sets the sum equal to 150, missing “more than the smallest,” and gets n = 48.
why.C: This is the middle integer.
why.D: Correct — with smallest n, n + (n + 2) + (n + 4) = n + 150, so 2n = 144 and n = 72. The largest is 76.

context: A straight angle is divided into two angles whose measures are in the ratio 1 : 5. What is the measure of the smaller angle?

why.A: Correct — the two angles make 6 equal parts of 180°, so each part is 30°.
why.B: This divides 180° by 5 instead of by the 1 + 5 = 6 parts.
why.C: This is the larger angle, 5 × 30°.
why.D: This splits 90° instead of 180°, as if the angles were complementary.

context: Two rays from the same point form an angle of 48°. What is the measure of the reflex angle formed by the same two rays?

why.A: This is the supplement, 180° − 48°. A reflex angle is more than 180°.
why.B: Correct — the two angles go all the way around the point, so the reflex angle is 360° − 48°.
why.C: This is the complement, 90° − 48°.
why.D: This adds 48° to a full turn instead of subtracting.

context: Parallel lines ℓ and m are cut by a transversal. Two corresponding angles measure (5x − 20)° and (3x + 30)°. What is the measure of each of these angles?

why.A: This is x, not the angle measure.
why.B: This is the supplement of the angle, the measure of its neighbor along the line.
why.C: Correct — corresponding angles are equal, so 5x − 20 = 3x + 30, x = 25, and 5(25) − 20 = 105.
why.D: This treats the angles as supplementary, solving 8x + 10 = 180. Corresponding angles are equal.

context: The sum of the interior angles of a polygon is 3 times the sum of its exterior angles. How many sides does the polygon have?

why.A: This stops at n − 2 = 6 without adding the 2 back.
why.B: This takes the exterior angles to add to 180°, getting (n − 2) × 180 = 540.
why.C: This reads the ratio 3 as the number of sides.
why.D: Correct — the exterior angles of any polygon add to 360°, so (n − 2) × 180 = 1,080 and n − 2 = 6.

context: Point M is the midpoint of segment AB. If AM = 2x + 3 and AB = 5x − 4, what is the length of AB?

why.A: Correct — AB is twice AM, so 2(2x + 3) = 5x − 4, giving x = 10 and AB = 5(10) − 4 = 46.
why.B: This is AM, half of AB.
why.C: This is x, not the length of AB.
why.D: This sets AM equal to AB, forgetting that AM is only half the segment.

context: Angle ABC is a right angle, and ray BD lies inside it. Angle ABD measures 12° more than twice angle DBC. What is the measure of angle ABD?

why.A: This is angle DBC, the smaller angle.
why.B: Correct — with angle DBC = y, (2y + 12) + y = 90, so y = 26 and angle ABD = 2(26) + 12 = 64.
why.C: This sets the two angles’ sum to 180°. Ray BD splits a right angle.
why.D: This removes the 12° and splits the rest evenly, (90 − 12) ÷ 2, ignoring “twice.”

context: The interior angles of a pentagon measure x°, (x + 10)°, (x + 20)°, (x + 30)° and (x + 40)°. What is the measure of the largest angle?

why.A: This is the smallest angle, x.
why.B: This is the average angle, 540 ÷ 5, which is the middle angle here, not the largest.
why.C: Correct — a pentagon’s angles add to (5 − 2) × 180 = 540°, so 5x + 100 = 540, x = 88 and the largest is 128°.
why.D: This uses 360° as the angle sum, which holds for a quadrilateral.

context: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. The bisectors of the two same-side interior angles meet at a point. What is the measure of the angle formed there by the two bisectors?

choices.text: It depends on the angle of the transversal.

why.A: This halves 90° again. The halves of the two angles add to 90°, and the angle between the bisectors is what remains of 180°.
why.B: This adds the two whole interior angles instead of their halves.
why.C: This assumes the answer changes with the transversal. The halves always add to 90°, whatever the angles are.
why.D: Correct — the same-side interior angles add to 180°, so their halves add to 90°. The third angle of the triangle the bisectors form is 180° − 90° = 90°.

context: Angles A and B are supplementary. The ratio of the complement of angle A to angle B is 1 : 4. What is the measure of angle A?

why.A: Correct — (90 − A)/(180 − A) = 1/4 gives 360 − 4A = 180 − A, so A = 60. Check: the complement is 30° and B is 120°.
why.B: This applies the 1 : 4 ratio to A and B themselves, skipping the complement.
why.C: This is the complement of A, not A.
why.D: This is angle B.

context: The angles of a triangle measure x°, x° and 100°. What is the value of x?

why.A: This finds 2x = 80 but does not divide by 2.
why.B: Correct — 2x + 100 = 180, so 2x = 80 and x = 40.
why.C: This halves the 100° angle instead of what remains of 180°.
why.D: This uses 360° as the angle sum, (360 − 100) ÷ 2.

context: In triangle ABC, AB = 6, BC = 8 and AC = 11. Which angle, if any, is a right angle?

why.A: This picks the angle opposite the longest side without checking. 6² + 8² would have to equal 11².
why.B: This takes the angle at the first-named vertex. A right angle, if there were one, would be opposite the longest side.
why.C: Correct — a right triangle needs 6² + 8² = 11², but 36 + 64 = 100, not 121. (Since 100 < 121, angle B is obtuse.)
why.D: This places the right angle at an end of the longest side, where the angles are the smallest.

context: A right triangle has legs of length 5 and 12. What is its area?

why.A: This multiplies the legs but does not take half.
why.B: This uses the hypotenuse, 13, in place of a leg: ½ × 5 × 13.
why.C: This adds the legs instead of multiplying them.
why.D: Correct — the legs are a base and height, so the area is ½ × 5 × 12 = 30.

context: A 30°-60°-90° triangle has a hypotenuse of length 12. What is its area?

why.A: Correct — the legs are 6 and 6√3, so the area is ½ × 6 × 6√3 = 18√3.
why.B: This multiplies the legs but does not take half.
why.C: This uses the hypotenuse as a leg, ½ × 6 × 12.
why.D: This drops the √3 from the longer leg, taking the legs as 6 and 6.

context: In triangle ABC, the exterior angle at vertex A measures 120°, and angle B measures 45°. What is the measure of angle C?

why.A: This subtracts both 120° and 45° from 180°, treating the exterior angle as an interior one.
why.B: Correct — an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, so 45 + C = 120.
why.C: This is interior angle A, 180° − 120°.
why.D: This adds the exterior angle and angle B.

context: Two similar triangles have areas of 16 and 49. The perimeter of the smaller triangle is 20. What is the perimeter of the larger triangle?

why.A: This scales the perimeter by the area ratio, 49/16. Perimeters scale by the square root of that ratio.
why.B: This adds the difference in areas, 33, to the perimeter.
why.C: Correct — the ratio of areas is 16 : 49, so the ratio of lengths is 4 : 7, and 20 × 7/4 = 35.
why.D: This adds 7 − 4 = 3 instead of multiplying by 7/4.

context: A 25-foot ladder leans against a wall with its base 7 feet from the wall. The base slides 8 feet farther from the wall. How many feet does the top of the ladder slide down?

why.A: This assumes the top slides down as far as the base slides out.
why.B: This is the new height of the top, not how far it moved.
why.C: This is the starting height of the top.
why.D: Correct — the top starts at √(625 − 49) = 24 feet. With the base 15 feet out, it is at √(625 − 225) = 20 feet, a drop of 4.

context: In right triangle ABC, the right angle is at C and AC = 6. The median from C to the hypotenuse AB has length 5. What is the length of BC?

why.A: Correct — the median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse, so AB = 10 and BC = √(100 − 36) = 8.
why.B: This computes √(36 − 25), treating AC as a hypotenuse and the median as a leg. The median runs to the midpoint of AB, not along a side.
why.C: This treats the median, 5, as the other leg and finds a hypotenuse, √(36 + 25).
why.D: This is AB. The median is half of the hypotenuse, not half of BC.

context: A right triangle has a perimeter of 30 and a hypotenuse of 13. What is its area?

why.A: This is ab, the product of the legs, without taking half.
why.B: Correct — the legs add to 17 and their squares add to 169. Since (a + b)² = a² + b² + 2ab, 289 = 169 + 2ab, so ab = 60 and the area is 30.
why.C: This is 2ab, which must be halved to get ab and halved again for the area.
why.D: This squares the leg sum and halves it, 17²/2, without removing the 169 from a² + b².

context: Two sides of an isosceles triangle have lengths 4 and 9. What is the perimeter of the triangle?

why.A: This uses sides 4, 4 and 9, which cannot form a triangle.
why.B: This adds only the two given sides.
why.C: Correct — sides of 4, 4 and 9 fail the triangle inequality because 4 + 4 < 9, so the sides must be 9, 9 and 4.
why.D: This accepts both cases without checking the triangle inequality.
